newsitem.title: EGYPT: Palestinians see economic meeting as weapon.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians see economic meeting as weapon.

text.p: Palestinian leaders said on Tuesday they wanted to use this week's economic conference in Cairo as a weapon in their negotiations with Israel.
But they denied asking other Arabs to boycott the Israeli delegation to the conference, saying any reluctance to meet Israelis was a spontaneous reaction to Israeli policy.

The Gulf state of Qatar put Palestinian hopes into practice, telling Israel on Tuesday it would not go ahead with plans to open a trade mission in the Jewish state unless progress was made at peace talks with the Palestinians.
Nabil Shaath, the Palestinian minister of planning and international cooperation, told a news conference: "We want the whole conference to be a card for putting pressure on Israel."

"We want this conference to say to Israel 'Look around you, there are 10,000 businesssmen here, talking about cooperation and development...but look behind you, if you don't carry out the commitments you made, you won't get any of it'," he added.
"We have, through this conference, to tell Israel that they cannot have peace for peace. It's only...peace for land," added Maher Masri, the Palestinian minister of economy and trade.
"They (Israelis) cannot have free trade with the Arab world and closure for the Palestinian people. This is the message of the business community that is being passed this day," he said.
Shaath said Israel was already feeling the consequences of the stalemate in Middle East peace talks after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power in June.

Netanyahu has backed out of a commitment to give back Arab land in return for peace and is trying to renegotiate the agreement the previous Israeli government made on an Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

"Israel has lost $1 billion in the form of investments that used to come to Israel. The shekel has fallen. Israel, in the time this government has been in power, has faced many difficulties in all aspects of the economy.

"It is not because we wanted that for Israel but because it was peace that brought that money to Israel in the beginning. After (the 1991 peace conference in) Madrid, Israel's growth rate doubled, the number of tourists doubled, it did normalisation from China and Senegal," he said.
Shaath and Masri both dissociated themselves from any attempt to give israel the cold shoulder.

"We are not trying to isolate Israel. It's only a reaction from all countries in the region to send a message -- 'If you want to go on with this process, you have to comply with the agreements.'," said Masri.

"We didn't ask anyone to boycott anyone. We came to this conference with a clear conscience, to tell the world we are going on with the peace process. but definitely there is a feeling of anger among the delegations," said Shaath.
Pressed on whether there was an organised boycott of Israel, he said: "As far as I know it is spontaneous."
Qatari Foreign Affairs Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jabr al-Thani, told a news conference:

"I met (Israeli Foreign Minister) David Levy half an hour ago and told him that unless there is progress on the Palestinian peace track we will not take action on our trade representation. We have frozen any developments in normalising our relations with Israel."
